lessons.title: Bet on What Never Changes
lessons.key_idea: Instead of predicting specific events, focus on the human behaviours that stay the same across every era.

lessons.title: Risk Is What You Don't See
lessons.key_idea: The biggest risks are the ones nobody anticipates, so prepare for surprises rather than trying to forecast them.

lessons.title: Happiness Is Expectations Minus Results
lessons.key_idea: How satisfied we feel depends less on our circumstances and more on how they compare with what we expected.

lessons.title: The Best Story Wins
lessons.key_idea: People are persuaded by compelling stories more than by facts, so the best idea doesn't always win.

lessons.title: Calm Plants the Seeds of Crazy
lessons.key_idea: Long stretches of stability make people comfortable taking bigger risks, which eventually creates the next crisis.

lessons.title: Overnight Tragedies, Long-Term Miracles
lessons.key_idea: Bad news hits suddenly and grabs attention, while progress compounds slowly and quietly, so we underrate how much things improve.

lessons.title: Build Room for Error
lessons.key_idea: Since the future is unpredictable, the wisest plan is to leave margin for error and accept volatility as the price of long-term reward.

plan.title: Same as Ever
plan.author: Morgan Housel
plan.confidence_note: I know the book's main chapters and core arguments well, but I am less certain of some specific anecdotes and exact wording, so lessons should stick to its central ideas.
plan.one_liner: Stop trying to predict the future. Learn the human behaviours that never change.
plan.summary: Morgan Housel argues that we waste energy trying to forecast events no one can foresee, when the smarter move is to understand the things about people that stay constant across history. Through short, story-driven chapters, he shows how greed, fear, and the stories we tell ourselves repeat in every era. The biggest risks are the ones nobody sees coming, so preparation beats prediction. Happiness depends less on what we have and more on what we expect. A compelling story often beats the plain truth. Long periods of calm quietly encourage the risky behaviour that ends them. Bad news arrives suddenly, while good news builds slowly and goes unnoticed. The practical takeaway is to build a life and finances with room for error, accept that volatility is the price of reward, and anchor decisions to what history shows never changes.
